facts: Dale Carnegie tells stories about Andrew Carnegie, the steel industrialist (no relation), to illustrate the power of names.
As a boy in Scotland, Andrew had a pair of rabbits that soon had a litter, and he had nothing to feed them.
He told the neighbourhood boys that if they gathered enough clover and dandelions to feed the rabbits, he would name the bunnies after them. It worked.
Years later, he wanted to sell steel rails to the Pennsylvania Railroad, whose president was J. Edgar Thomson.
He built a steel mill in Pittsburgh and named it the Edgar Thomson Steel Works.
When the Pennsylvania Railroad needed rails, it bought them from Carnegie.
Dale Carnegie also mentions Jim Farley, a political organizer said to know the first names of 50,000 people.
Principle: remember that a person's name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language.
tension: A boy with hungry rabbits and no food discovers a principle that later helps him sell steel.
opening_idea: A Scottish boy needs food for his rabbits, and offers the neighbourhood kids something money can't buy.

lessons.idea: People care deeply about their own names.
lessons.anchor: Boys gathering food for rabbits named after them

lessons.idea: Remembering names is a learnable discipline.
